text:
Live Updates: Jensen Huang Resigns From Nvidia After Affairs
The longtime head of the chip-making colossus admitted to an affair with a woman identified as a spy for China. He was also said to have had a relationship with an executive who reported to him.
Latest
Jensen Huang, the co-founder and chief executive of the Silicon Valley chip giant Nvidia, resigned on Thursday, according to the company’s board of directors, capping a swift, stunning fall for one of the most powerful figures in the A.I. boom. His departure came after revelations that he had extramarital affairs with an executive who reported to him and with a woman whom U.S. intelligence agencies concluded was spying for China.
Colette Kress, Nvidia’s chief financial officer, will serve as interim chief executive while the search for a permanent replacement is carried out, Nvidia’s 10-member board said in a statement. In a note to Nvidia employees, Ms. Kress said she believes “deeply in this company” and called its employees “our greatest strength.”
Mr. Huang’s exit, which followed a lengthy board meeting on Wednesday, opens an uncertain chapter for Nvidia, the premier maker of artificial intelligence chips, and will have widespread ripple effects. Its shares plunged more than 10 percent at the start of trading, weighing on the broader market.
Over three decades, Mr. Huang, 63, built Nvidia into one of the world’s most valuable public companies, controlling an estimated 90 percent of the market for the advanced chips that are an essential component of the A.I. projects driving the U.S. economy — and are at the center of the U.S.-China tussle for dominance in A.I.
A series of reports by The New York Times showed that Mr. Huang had an affair with a Chinese businesswoman who goes by Alice Huang, who had been recruited by China’s main spy agency to gather information on Mr. Huang, and that President Trump had been warned about the relationship but took no action. Ms. Huang has not responded to requests for comment.
Though Nvidia had said that it had “no reason to believe” that Mr. Huang had compromised national security or company secrets, its board, with a track record of deference to its celebrity C.E.O., opened an investigation. The company’s share price plunged in after-hours trading on Wednesday as the board met to consider Mr. Huang’s future, and continued to slide on Thursday.
China has rejected the espionage claims. U.S. officials suspect that Megaspeed, the Singaporean company where Ms. Huang was a top executive, has helped smuggle restricted chips into China. China’s embassy has called the allegations “smears.”
Here’s what else to know:
- A second affair: Mr. Huang also had an extramarital relationship with an executive who reported to him, according to five people who worked at the company, The Times reported on Wednesday. Under Nvidia’s code of conduct, employees are told to “avoid situations where our actions create conflict” including “personal relationships,” and the company states that it “promptly investigates reports of misconduct.” Read more ›
- C.E.O.’s influence: Among global tech executives, few have had as much sway as Mr. Huang over Mr. Trump’s approach to A.I. and China. He persuaded the president to roll back a ban on chip sales to China, and Nvidia has donated at least $20 million to a fund for Mr. Trump’s White House ballroom project.
- Trump’s response: Mr. Trump has defended Mr. Huang over the past week, calling him an “honorable man” and saying that Mr. Huang had told him he was not aware that Ms. Huang was an intelligence operative for Beijing. The president is scheduled to travel to China next week, and he said on Monday that he did not plan to bring the Nvidia matter up in talks with China’s leader, Xi Jinping.
It seems crazy to suggest that the downfall of one chief executive could have macroeconomic implications, but in this case it might be true.
Jensen Huang, as has been widely discussed in recent days, ran Nvidia almost single-handedly and was unusually central to his company’s success. Nvidia, in turn, has been unusually central to the artificial intelligence boom — not just developing the chips that run most A.I. models, but also helping to finance the data center build out.
And that build out has become a crucial driver of U.S. economic growth while some other sectors are struggling. Moreover, Mr. Huang’s ouster comes at what was already a delicate time for the A.I. industry. There have been signs in recent months that investors are growing more skeptical that companies will be able to deliver returns that justify the huge investments they are making in A.I., or at least that those returns could take longer than expected to materialize.
And Democrats’ sweeping victories in last week’s midterm elections could lead to new restrictions on data center construction, which could jeopardize the industry’s boom. In the past, when confidence in the A.I. story has wavered, Mr. Huang and Nvidia have often been the ones to calm doubts, reporting huge sales figures or stepping in to provide financing to data center projects whose future seemed in jeopardy.
This time around, it isn’t clear who will fill the void.
The descent of Jensen Huang
Jensen Huang’s ouster at Nvidia also leaves a vacuum in A.I. policy in Washington. He has been a leading and influential voice in favor of opening sales of chips to China and against regulations on safety.
Already, members of Congress from both parties are calling for legislation to tighten export controls over A.I. chips to China after revelations of Huang’s affair with a Chinese spy. He was one of the strongest voices, lobbying personally at the Trump White House, to reverse export controls on chips. With Democrats soon to hold majorities in both houses of Congress, there is likely to be greater pressure on the Commerce Department to enforce rules and to tighten sales bans to China.
The appointment of Colette Kress, who has been Nvidia’s chief financial officer, to lead the company on an interim basis will likely raise questions in Washington about how much she was aware of the company’s dealings with Megaspeed, the Singaporean data center firm that was led by the alleged Chinese spy whom Huang had an affair with.
Late last year, as U.S. government concerns were rising about Megaspeed, Nvidia suddenly changed how it recorded its global revenue, making it harder to see how much of its sales were being booked through Southeast Asia and Singapore. It also remains to be seen what Kress’s attitude will be toward issues like alleged chip smuggling and export controls.
News that Jensen Huang, the co-founder of Nvidia, was having an affair with a woman believed to be Chinese spy has sent shock waves through the tech world, the U.S. government and the wider economy.
Mr. Huang served as Nvidia’s chief executive from 1993, when he co-founded the company, until his resignation on Thursday. He rocketed to prominence during the A.I. boom as Nvidia’s advanced chips became a crucial technology, making it one of the world’s most valuable companies. Mr. Huang, 63, has close ties to President Trump and has frequently appeared alongside him.
Here’s how the events unfolded.
2023: A Chinese executive named Alice Huang sets up a data firm in Singapore called Megaspeed. The company, which originally had Chinese owners, would soon buy billions of dollars’ worth of Nvidia’s artificial intelligence chips. In May 2023, Nvidia reaches $1 trillion in value.
December 2023: While it’s not clear when Mr. Huang, who is married, met Ms. Huang, they were acquainted by December 2023, when they had dinner with colleagues at a restaurant in Singapore. In June 2024, they were seen socializing at an event in Taipei.
June 2024 to June 2025: A Megaspeed subsidiary receives more than 200 shipments of Nvidia A.I. equipment.
July 2025: Nvidia becomes the first public company ever to be worth $4 trillion.
September 2025: The U.S. government, through the Commerce Department, begins an investigation into Megaspeed, examining whether some of the Nvidia chips it bought were sent to China, a possible violation of U.S. export controls.
Early 2025: Weeks after Mr. Trump begins his second term, Mr. Huang visits the White House to meet with him for the first time.
March 2025: Ms. Huang visits Nvidia’s headquarters in Santa Clara, Calif.
April 2025: During a dinner for donors at Mar-a-Lago, Mr. Huang makes a case to Mr. Trump for allowing chip companies like Nvidia to do business with China. The same month, the White House shuts down Nvidia’s sales to China, strengthening Biden-era regulations that put limits on the sale of A.I. technology.
May 2025: Ms. Huang and Mr. Huang dine with others in Taipei. They pose for a photo together, and she kisses him on the cheek.
July 2025: The Trump administration reverses course and assures Nvidia that it will be granted a license to sell certain chips to China.
October 2025: U.S. intelligence officials tell Mr. Trump that Mr. Huang has a relationship with Ms. Huang, who they describe as a Chinese intelligence asset. Mr. Trump chooses not to take any action.
December 2025: Mr. Trump approves the sale of more powerful Nvidia chips to China.
May 2026: Secretary of State Marco Rubio warns U.S. officials that Mr. Huang is in a close relationship with a Chinese spy. The same month, Mr. Trump invites Mr. Huang to join him on a state visit to Beijing.
October 2026: Mr. Huang’s affair with Ms. Huang is reported in The New York Times.
November 2026: After Mr. Huang admits the affair, Nvidia’s board says it will conduct an investigation. The New York Times later reports that Mr. Huang also had a relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care, who reports to him.
On Nov. 12, Nvidia’s board of directors announces that Mr. Huang has resigned.
President Trump has been curiously silent about this since we and others reported that the Nvidia board was assessing Jensen Huang’s fate. Trump and Huang had developed a close relationship. Among global tech executives, few have had as much sway as Huang over Trump’s approach to A.I. and China.
It’s not entirely clear how the market reaction will play out. Nvidia’s initial move lower appears to be dragging the broader market down, too. But some analysts had already begun noting yesterday that this leadership change does not fundamentally change Nvidia’s very successful business model, suggesting the stock should recover. It’s also not clear whether this creates a competitive advantage for the other chipmakers, offering a tailwind to their stock prices, or whether they, too, will simply get caught up in the sell-off, which appears more likely in the immediate term.
Nvidia’s stock slumped more than 10 percent at the opening bell on Thursday. The move lower tugged on broader U.S. indexes — the S&P 500 opened nearly 1 percent in the red while the tech-heavy Nasdaq fell more than 1 percent.
S&P 500
In a note to Nvidia employees, Colette Kress, the interim chief executive officer, said she believes “deeply in this company” and its employees. “This company has achieved so much because of the work that all of you bring to it every single day,” she said. “You are our greatest strength.”
Kress said there would be a company meeting on Nov. 18 to discuss its future.
The speed with which Nvidia’s board of directors acted may be surprising, given its long history with Huang. Its 10 members had served for a combined 161 years. During that time, Huang’s big bets usually paid off for Nvidia and the people backing him.
Two board members, Mark A. Stevens and Tench Coxe, were early investors in Nvidia and the second and third largest individual shareholders in the company after Huang, with stakes each worth billions of dollars.
Huang had viewed Nvidia’s board primarily as a governance requirement, rather than as an important part of the company’s strategy or execution, according to three former employees.
The ouster of Huang is portentous for the alliance between the Trump administration and the so-called “tech right,” or the leaders of Silicon Valley’s recent conservative inflection. Huang himself did not do much political giving or display overt partisan leanings. But he was a leader of the tech billionaire class’s political push, which included crafting a grow-at-all-costs A.I. agenda that the billionaires argued was good for the U.S. (and was certainly good for Nvidia.)
With Huang’s exit, and after last week’s repudiation of Republicans in the midterms, we are entering a different era in Silicon Valley and Washington.
It seems crazy to suggest that the downfall of one chief executive could have macroeconomic implications, but in this case it might be true. Jensen Huang ran Nvidia almost single-handedly and was central to its success. Nvidia, in turn, has been central to the A.I. boom — not just developing the chips that run most A.I. models, but also helping to finance the building of data centers, a crucial driver of U.S. economic growth.
And it was already a delicate time for the A.I. industry: There are signs that investors are growing more skeptical that companies can deliver returns that justify the massive investments they are making in A.I. And Democrats’ sweeping midterm victories could lead to new restrictions on data center construction.
Nvidia recognized Huang in a statement, saying, “Jensen’s contributions to Nvidia are profound. Nvidia is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world. The board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry.”
The company’s press release announcing his departure did not include a statement from Huang.
It’s unclear what the next steps are for Jensen Huang, who is 63. He worked at Nvidia for more than three decades after co-founding the company at age 30. Elon Musk, the chief executive of Tesla and SpaceX, suggested on social media last night that it would be “an honor” to hire Mr. Huang, though he did not say for what position.
For some perspective on how much Huang’s resignation could matter to the U.S. economy, Goldman Sachs estimates that spending on A.I.-related hardware and intellectual property could reach $1.4 trillion in 2027, up from $900 billion this year. That is 4 percent of the United States’ entire expected economic output. Many of those data centers are filled with Nvidia chips, or indirectly financed by the company.
The board of directors appointed Harvey C. Jones as Nvidia’s first-ever chairman. Jones has years of experience in the chip industry, having served as chief executive and executive chairman of Synopsys.
One of the immediate concerns in the wake of Jensen Huang’s resignation is whether it will lead to an exodus of talent from Nvidia. The company is made up of longtime loyalists to Huang. He was not only revered as a visionary; he made many of them wealthier than they ever imagined. In 2022, the company was worth $305 billion. By 2026, it was flirting with a valuation of $6 trillion.
Colette Kress, a longtime Nvidia executive, was appointed by the board of directors as the interim chief executive officer.
In a note to Nvidia employees on Thursday, Ms. Kress said she believes “deeply in this company” and each of its employees. “This company has achieved so much because of the work that all of you bring to it every single day,” she said.
Nvidia veteran: Ms. Kress, the company’s chief financial officer, joined Nvidia in 2013. She has worked closely with Mr. Huang as the company transitioned from a niche maker of graphics processors used for video games to a company at the center of the artificial intelligence boom. She previously worked for Cisco and Microsoft. She has an undergraduate degree in finance from the University of Arizona and a M.B.A. from Southern Methodist University. She will remain the company’s finance chief while serving as interim chief executive.
Closeness to Jensen Huang: Mr. Huang interviewed 22 candidates before hiring Ms. Kress as chief financial officer. At the time, Ms. Kress’s young sons, who were avid gamers, encouraged her to join Nvidia. During her first week on the job, Ms. Kress asked Mr. Huang how long he thought he would want her in the role. “I said, ‘For as long as we shall live and death do us part,’” Mr. Jensen said in a podcast appearance this year.
China: During her time as chief financial officer, Ms. Kress expressed concerns about the financial impact of American policies that restrict Nvidia sales to China. In 2023, she said on a call with financial analysts that China accounted for 20 to 25 percent of the company’s data center revenue. In addition to lost sales, she has said the policies risk strengthening Nvidia’s competitors in China.
Liaison to Wall Street: As chief financial officer, one of Ms. Kress’s main responsibilities was communicating with Wall Street and Nvidia’s investors. On quarterly earnings calls, Ms. Kress delivered a rosy message as Nvidia’s revenue and stock price soared. In 2013, Nvidia’s sales were $4.28 billion. In the most recent fiscal year, its annual sales reached $215.9 billion.
Personal Wealth: Ms. Kress has benefited from Nvidia’s skyrocketing stock price. She owned roughly 4.44 million shares, according to Nvidia’s most recent annual report, worth about $772 million.
Nvidia’s stock has plunged following the news of Huang’s departure. Shares have fallen more than 11 percent in premarket trading, wiping out over $1 trillion from the company’s market value this month.
Jensen Huang led Nvidia with an executive team of more than 60 direct reports, placing him at the center of day-to-day operations at the company. That flat structure will be difficult to unwind and could complicate a transition to new leadership.
On a podcast in 2023, Huang dismissed traditional organizational charts, saying that “none of that stuff makes any sense to me.” He led Nvidia largely through meetings that focused on particular projects and included people from all levels of the company, from recent college graduates to top executives. Huang said last year that he reads several thousand emails a day from people across the company.
Jensen Huang was fighting hard to hang onto his role with the company he founded, according to several people briefed on the discussions. But an interim plan for the chief financial officer, Colette Kress, to take over Nvidia was well underway yesterday.
Nvidia’s shares plummeted Thursday, sending tremors through global markets, as the company’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, stepped down from his role.
Shares in Nvidia dropped more than 10 percent when markets opened for trading on Thursday, extending a drop that has wiped out more than $1 trillion from the company’s market value this month alone.
The company’s board named Colette Kress, the company’s chief financial officer, as its interim chief executive.
With the change in Nvidia’s leadership, investors face uncertainty about the sustainability of the artificial intelligence trade and how the problems inside one of the technology industry’s most important companies could affect the broader economy.
The fallout could be seen in markets around the world, although the effects appeared limited. Major market indexes in Asia, where many of Nvidia’s partners and rivals in the artificial intelligence industry are based, mostly declined. Taiwan’s TSMC, which produces chips designed by Nvidia, fell nearly 2 percent. But South Korea’s Samsung, which competes with Nvidia on some business lines, gained 1 percent.
European stock indexes, which are less heavily exposed to A.I., were flat on Thursday. But shares in the region’s largest tech company, ASML of the Netherlands, fell nearly 2 percent.
In the United States, the tech-heavy Nasdaq slipped more than 1 percent when markets began trading on Thursday.
Shares in some of Nvidia’s U.S. rivals were set to climb: AMD rose more than 2 percent and Broadcom gained nearly 6 percent on Thursday. The broader S&P 500 index opened slightly lower.
Mr. Huang, who co-founded Nvidia in 1993, has become one of the most influential forces in the A.I. boom, which has helped to drive U.S. stock markets to new highs in recent years.
Nvidia’s board deliberations came after revelations that Mr. Huang had an affair with an executive who reports to him as well as with a woman whom U.S. intelligence has identified as a Chinese spy.
Some market analysts covering Nvidia have begun to downgrade their forecasts for the company’s stock. Though the chipmaker is expected to remain a critical part of the A.I. build-out, some noted rising concerns about the company’s governance and lack of a clear succession plan. They argued that these revelations have fundamentally changed Mr. Huang’s position in the tech world and it was unclear what the implications of a change in his role at Nvidia could be.
Analysts at Bernstein downgraded Nvidia and sharply lowered their target for its share price. “Our gut tells us that we probably haven’t yet fully probed the depths of what might be found here,” they wrote. “We’ve had enough, and prefer to watch from the sidelines.”
Analysts at RBC Capital Markets also slashed their forecast for the stock, citing the lack of formal succession plan for the chief executive position. “Whether any individual can replicate Huang’s singular combination of technical vision, ecosystem-building acumen and ability to serve as the global face of the A.I. revolution remains an open question,” they noted.
Other analysts, including those at Wells Fargo and Mizuho, maintained their bullish views on Nvidia, but said it was increasingly likely that Mr. Huang might not be chief executive for much longer.
Nvidia’s stock is down about a third from its peak at the start of October, putting the company deep in a bear market, defined as a drop of 20 percent or more from a recent high.
Nvidia became the world’s largest public company, by market value, for the first time in 2024, exerting an outsize influence over major indexes like the Nasdaq Composite and the S&P 500. Analysts still expect Nvidia to make a profit of well over $200 billion this year, with its chips in high demand as tech companies rush to build giant A.I. data centers.
During last week’s market turmoil, Nvidia fell below Apple as the world’s biggest public company.
Jensen Huang, the leader of Nvidia who is under investigation for an affair with a woman who U.S. intelligence determined is a Chinese spy, also had an extramarital relationship with an executive who reports to him, according to five people who worked at the company.
The relationship, which has not been previously reported, was with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care, said the people, who spoke under the condition of anonymity to describe sensitive information. Under Nvidia’s code of conduct, employees are told to “avoid situations where our actions create conflict” including “personal relationships,” and the company states that it “promptly investigates reports of misconduct.” Many corporations have policies against managers having relationships with subordinates.
Mr. Huang, 63, and Ms. Powell, 48, were captured on video being affectionate at a San Jose, Calif., hotel during a Nvidia conference in March, according to two of the people who worked at the company. The New York Times has not seen the video.
Both Mr. Huang and Ms. Powell are married to other people.
Mr. Huang, who co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and has turned it into the premier supplier of artificial intelligence chips, has been under intensifying scrutiny. Last month, The Times reported that a Chinese executive he had become close to had been identified by U.S. officials as a Chinese intelligence asset.
This month, after Mr. Huang acknowledged the affair, Nvidia’s board opened an investigation into the matter that is being led by the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz. The Republican leaders of three influential House committees have also asked Mr. Huang to appear for a closed-door briefing on his interactions with the woman, who goes by the name Alice Huang.
China has denied the espionage claims. Ms. Huang, the Chinese executive accused of spying for Beijing, has not responded to requests for comment.
When reached by phone Wednesday and asked about his relationship with Ms. Powell, Mr. Huang said, “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly.” He then hung up.
Nvidia declined to provide a statement. Ms. Powell did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The company’s shares fell about 8 percent in after-hours trading.
Mr. Huang’s relationship with Ms. Powell has been discussed inside the company, the five people said.
Ms. Powell joined Nvidia in 2008. She oversees programs that could apply Nvidia’s chip technology to higher education and health care, particularly medical imaging devices, according to the company’s website.
Ms. Powell has risen through Nvidia’s ranks. She was promoted to senior director of artificial intelligence business development in 2016, according to her LinkedIn. By late 2017, she was appointed vice president of health care. She attends technology conferences around the world, and delivers speeches on behalf of the company.
In March, Ms. Powell appeared at GTC, Nvidia’s annual developer conference in San Jose, where she spoke about using A.I. to aid in breakthroughs in health care and biology. Her presentation used cartoon depictions of Mr. Huang.
During the conference, Nvidia executives were at a nearby hotel for meetings. Mr. Huang and Ms. Powell were seen being affectionate at the hotel. One bystander captured the interaction on their phone, three people briefed on the incident said.
Mr. Huang’s security workers witnessed the bystander with the phone and sequestered the person, the people said. The workers then asked the person to sign a nondisclosure agreement.
Mr. Huang is among a long list of chief executives of American companies who have had relationships with subordinates. Brian Krzanich resigned in 2018 from Intel, the chip maker, after acknowledging a “past consensual relationship” with an employee.
The following year, McDonald’s removed Steve Easterbrook as its chief executive and later sued him after learning he had violated corporate policies by maintaining sexual relationships with multiple employees.
In November 2021, Jensen Huang attended the annual dinner held by the Semiconductor Industry Association in San Jose, Calif. That night, the trade group gave Mr. Huang, the chief executive of Nvidia, its highest honor, named for the Intel co-founder Robert Noyce.
Mr. Huang arrived early with his wife, Lori Huang, and quickly headed to the bar at the pre-dinner reception, saying the event was the first time he had been out of his house since the Covid lockdown began in March 2020. He introduced Ms. Huang to reporters who clustered nearby, but they mainly talked to him.
By the time Mr. Huang received the award, two hours had passed. The Nvidia leader walked onstage with a bottle of red wine and two glasses, sharing them with a moderator and taking the conversation into unexpected topics. Throughout, Ms. Huang remained in the background.
For more than 40 years, Ms. Huang has been by Mr. Huang’s side as he built his fledgling chip start-up into one of the most valuable companies in the world. Nvidia’s success turned Mr. Huang into an international business star. His face is on sweaters, his signature leather jackets have become collectors items, and his net worth has soared to nearly $150 billion.
By contrast, Ms. Huang stayed far from the spotlight.
That changed this week, when Mr. Huang, 63, revealed he had an affair with an executive identified by the U.S. government as a Chinese spy. In his admission, which he shared in a message to Nvidia employees, Mr. Huang apologized to his wife, as well as his two children, who both work at Nvidia, thrusting them into the limelight.
The bombshell news had implications for U.S. national security and the economy. Nvidia’s role as the A.I. industry’s main supplier of chips makes Mr. Huang a crucial linchpin for an industry that has come to dominate the stock market.
It also has ramifications for his personal life. Mr. Huang’s admission has fueled speculation about the fate of his 41-year marriage with Ms. Huang, 64. She is president of the Jen-Hsun Lori Huang Foundation, which had $9 billion in assets as of 2024, including $6 billion in fresh funding that year. Of Mr. Huang’s 922 million Nvidia shares, more than half belong to a trust where Mr. Huang and Ms. Huang are the co-trustees, according to financial filings. She is also the sole controller of a trust that owns around $5 billion worth of Nvidia shares.
Ms. Huang joins a small group of tech titan spouses who have had to grapple with public infidelity. The list includes MacKenzie Scott, the ex-wife of the Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, and Melinda French Gates, ex-wife of the Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates. The billionaire ex-wife of a tech mogul has become such a fixture in American pop culture that it has inspired characters in “The Devil Wears Prada 2” and the Maya Rudolph comedy “Loot.”
Ms. Huang’s public profile stands out among the current and former spouses of powerful business leaders because of how private she has been. She has not promoted her philanthropic work in interviews or on the conference circuit.
“Lori is unusually modest by the standards of billionaire couples,” said George Rush, who formerly coauthored Rush & Molloy, a long-running gossip column at The Daily News.
That adds further intrigue to the political and economic consequences of the affair, Mr. Rush noted. “Bezos and Gates didn’t have this dynamic, where the relationship could move markets and have this global fallout,” he said. “It is one of a kind.”
Nvidia declined to comment and Ms. Huang did not respond to a request for comment. (China has rejected the espionage claims. Alice Huang, the Chinese executive accused of spying for Beijing, has not responded to requests for comment.)
Similar to other tech billionaire spouses like Ms. Scott, Ms. Huang was crucial to the start of her husband’s company.
She met Mr. Huang as one of a handful of women studying engineering at Oregon State University in the early 1980s. Mr. Huang was her lab partner in an electrical engineering fundamentals class, and he convinced her to join him for a weekly study date. He later called meeting her “the most important, single event of OSU, and of my life.”
After the pair graduated and married, they moved to Silicon Valley to work as microchip designers. Both were known as gifted engineers. Ms. Huang worked at Silicon Graphics, a hardware and software maker, where her salary was higher than Mr. Huang’s at LSI Logic, a semiconductor company, he said in a 2023 profile in The New Yorker.
But the couple struggled to find the right child care, according to “The Thinking Machine,” a biography of Mr. Huang. Just before he co-founded Nvidia in 1993, Ms. Huang gave up her career to raise their children, Spencer and Madison. While Mr. Huang missed their karate tournaments to build his company, Ms. Huang never complained, he recalled in May on the podcast How I Built This With Guy Raz. “That’s the gift that she gave me.”
Mr. Huang has frequently shared a warm reverence for Ms. Huang in interviews. “It’s good to have someone in your life who unconditionally believes in you, who believes you’re doing your best,” he said in an interview with a publication run by Oregon State University in 2014. “You need people like that, and Lori’s always been that person for me — ever since I was 18, she was there believing in me and knowing I could do it. Even when I had self-doubts, she didn’t.”
When Mr. Huang’s Nvidia shares made him wealthy, the family set up an endowment that ballooned alongside their net worth. The foundation has donated to the San Francisco Opera and acquired computing power to donate to universities and nonprofits. The Huangs have sidestepped political donations.
Through it all, Ms. Huang was a frequent presence at Mr. Huang’s public events, including state dinners, conference appearances and celebrations of the couple’s donations to Stanford University and Oregon State University. She generally stayed in the background while he gave speeches and hobnobbed with industry executives and reporters.
“She’s been to every conference, every speech, you know, and every moment of Nvidia, she was there,” he said in an interview this year with CNA, an Asian news network. “Lori’s been with me for a long time, our whole life.”
She even helped shape his public image. Along with her daughter Madison, she dressed Mr. Huang in a designer leather jacket that has become his trademark look. Madison joined Nvidia in 2020 and Spencer joined the company in 2022. Madison’s husband, Nico Caprez, also works there.
Mr. Huang ended his message to Nvidia employees about the affair with a request: “My family bears no responsibility for my choices. I do. Please give them privacy.”
Georgia Gee contributed research.
